paras: The killing of Edwin Nicholson took place on August 15, 1910, on the Hillsboro road in West Raleigh, North Carolina, when a guard shot Nicholson, a Black county convict, as he ran from a Wake county road force. The guard, R. M. Saunders, fired on the foreman's order, and the coroner decided no inquest was needed. A wire version circulated beyond the state, built around Nicholson's reported remark that he would rather be dead than alive.

Nicholson was serving six months on the county roads for robbing, or attempting to break into, the cash drawer of a Raleigh grocery, given in one report as W. B. Mann's store. The Caucasian of Clinton called the offense larceny and said Nicholson had once lived in Raleigh, left some years before, and returned within the past month. He had been on the road force only a few days, working with about twenty-four convicts who were widening the road between the city limits and the Fair grounds.

About 1 p.m., just after dinner, Nicholson broke from the squad and ran up Hillsboro Street toward the city rather than into the woods along the road. According to the Richmond Virginian's Raleigh correspondent, the guard called on him to halt, then asked the foreman whether to shoot, and the foreman said "shoot." After Nicholson had run about seventy-five yards, the rifle ball struck him in the back of the head and killed him instantly.

Saunders gave a statement that, according to The Caucasian, the supervisor and others present confirmed. The coroner held that an inquest was not necessary, "since the shooting was apparently justified," and no report of a charge against the guard appears in the coverage.

Only white papers carried the story, as far as the coverage shows, and every account rests on the guard's and officials' version. Raleigh specials to the Richmond Times-Dispatch and Richmond Virginian on August 16 ran it as "Negro Convict Shot to Death" and "Convict Is Shot Trying to Escape," alongside other Raleigh news. The Times-Dispatch added that "some believe that he really courted death by running in the open."

An Asheville-datelined wire carried the same idea further, opening with his declaration "that he would sooner be dead than alive." It ran the same day in the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Bluefield Evening Leader and the Newark Evening Star, the last under the headline "Wanted to Die; Gets Wish." In North Carolina, The Robesonian printed a one-sentence notice and The Caucasian wrote that the guard "was compelled to fire" after Nicholson refused repeated orders to halt.

reader.title: Killing of Edwin Nicholson
bases: A convict guard on a Wake county road force shot a fleeing Black prisoner, by the foreman's or supervisor's order; no crowd was involved (A4, A5, A7).

Separate Raleigh specials to two Richmond papers and a North Carolina local item agree that Nicholson was shot dead by guard R. M. Saunders while fleeing a convict road squad on August 15 (A4, A5, A7).

accounts.label: Guard and supervisor (Raleigh local report)
accounts.gist: Nicholson refused repeated orders to halt and the guard, acting on the supervisor's orders, was 'compelled to fire'; the supervisor and others present were said to confirm Saunders's statement.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondents
accounts.gist: Nicholson broke from a road force after dinner and ran up Hillsboro Street toward the city; the guard called halt, asked the foreman whether to shoot, and on his word shot Nicholson in the back of the head.

accounts.label: Wire report (Asheville dateline)
accounts.gist: Nicholson, having said he would sooner be dead than alive, ran down the open road rather than into the woods, which led to 'the belief that he courted death.'

framing.detail: The Asheville wire ran under 'Negro Shot To Death' (A1), 'Convict Killed by Prison Guard' (A2) and 'Wanted to Die; Gets Wish' (A3), framing the death around his reported wish to die.

The Raleigh specials ('Negro Convict Shot to Death', 'Convict Is Shot Trying to Escape') gave a factual account bundled with other Raleigh news, the Times-Dispatch adding that 'some believe' he courted death.
The Caucasian said the guard 'was compelled to fire' and repeated that the shooting was 'apparently justified'.
